title: What happens if you call `start()` twice on the same Thread (`IllegalThreadStateException`)?
shortTitle: What happens if you call start() twice on the same Thread?

s1_definition.profdef: Calling `start()` a second time on the same `Thread` object throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. A Thread is a one-shot object whose lifecycle moves from NEW to RUNNABLE to TERMINATED and can never return to NEW. The first `start()` transitions the thread out of the NEW state, and `start()` is only legal from the NEW state, so a second call, whether while the thread is still running or after it has terminated, violates that precondition and throws the unchecked `IllegalThreadStateException`. To run the same work again you must create a fresh Thread, or use an executor that manages reusable worker threads.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a Thread as a single-use entry pass at National Bank of India's secure data centre. The first time you swipe the pass at the gate, it activates and lets you in, and once used it is permanently marked as spent. If you try to swipe the very same pass again, the gate rejects it with an error, because a pass is valid for exactly one entry and cannot be reset. To enter again you need a brand-new pass. A Thread object is that one-use pass: start works once, and a second swipe throws the error.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Thread can be started exactly once; a second start throws IllegalThreadStateException, so create a new Thread or use an executor to run the work again.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Calling `start()` a second time on the same `Thread` object throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. A Thread is a one-shot object whose lifecycle moves from NEW to RUNNABLE to TERMINATED and can never return to NEW. The first `start()` transitions the thread out of the NEW state, and `start()` is only legal from the NEW state, so a second call, whether while the thread is still running or after it has terminated, violates that precondition and throws the unchecked `IllegalThreadStateException`. To run the same work again you must create a fresh Thread, or use an executor that manages reusable worker threads.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a Thread as a single-use entry pass at National Bank of India's secure data centre. The first time you swipe the pass at the gate, it activates and lets you in, and once used it is permanently marked as spent. If you try to swipe the very same pass again, the gate rejects it with an error, because a pass is valid for exactly one entry and cannot be reset. To enter again you need a brand-new pass. A Thread object is that one-use pass: start works once, and a second swipe throws the error.

**One line to remember:** A Thread can be started exactly once; a second start throws IllegalThreadStateException, so create a new Thread or use an executor to run the work again.

sections.s2_technical:
A Java Thread object represents one operating-system-backed thread of execution and has a strict lifecycle. When you construct a Thread it is in the NEW state, meaning it has been created but not yet scheduled. Calling start transitions it to RUNNABLE, at which point the JVM creates the underlying native thread and eventually runs the thread's run method. When run completes, normally or by exception, the thread moves to TERMINATED, also called DEAD. Crucially there is no transition back to NEW from any later state. The lifecycle is one-directional.

The start method is defined to be valid only when the thread is in the NEW state. Internally it checks the thread's state, and if the thread has already been started it throws IllegalThreadStateException, which is an unchecked RuntimeException, specifically a subclass of IllegalArgumentException in the class hierarchy. This check fires in two situations: calling start again while the thread is still running, and calling start again after the thread has already finished and terminated. In both cases the thread is no longer in NEW, so start is illegal. The exception is not about concurrency timing; it is about the lifecycle precondition, so it is deterministic.

A common confusion is between calling start twice versus calling run twice. The run method is just an ordinary method; calling it directly does not start a new thread at all, it executes the body synchronously on the current thread, and you can call run as many times as you like because it has no lifecycle check. That is also why calling run directly is almost always a bug when you meant to start concurrency: it runs the code on the calling thread instead of a new one. The lifecycle protection lives in start, not run.

The reason the design is one-shot is that a thread is tied to a native operating-system thread resource and to a specific execution context, and reusing the same Thread object for multiple independent runs would complicate state, naming, thread-local storage, and interruption semantics. Rather than make Thread reusable, the Java concurrency model separates the work from the worker. You express the work as a Runnable or Callable, and you submit it to an ExecutorService, which maintains a pool of reusable worker threads. The pool runs your task on some worker thread and then returns that worker to the pool for the next task, so the reuse happens at the pool level while each Thread object itself is still started only once by the pool's internals. This is why in production you almost never create and start raw Thread objects; you submit tasks to an executor.

The senior-level practices are concrete. If you need to run the same logic repeatedly, do not keep a Thread field and try to restart it; instead create a new Thread each time, or far better, keep the logic in a Runnable and submit it to an ExecutorService such as a fixed thread pool, which also bounds resource usage. You handle the terminated case by checking Thread state with getState if you must, but you design so that you never attempt a restart. In banking systems where background jobs like settlement sweeps run on schedules, you use a scheduled executor that submits the task repeatedly to pooled threads, never a single Thread that you try to start again, because the second start would throw and could crash the scheduler.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a nightly settlement sweep. An early version created one Thread for the sweep and, to run it again for a retry, called start on the same Thread object a second time, which threw IllegalThreadStateException and aborted the retry. This is exactly the one-shot lifecycle rule: the Thread had already left the NEW state, so a second start is illegal.

Problem 2 — The team must run the sweep repeatedly, on a schedule and on retries, without ever hitting the restart error. This is exactly what an ExecutorService provides: the sweep logic lives in a Runnable, and the pool runs it as many times as needed on reusable worker threads.

We will build a runnable demo that first reproduces the error by starting the same Thread twice, then shows the correct pattern of submitting the sweep Runnable to a fixed thread pool multiple times without any lifecycle error. The code includes a SettlementSweep Runnable, a demo that triggers the exception deliberately and catches it, and the executor-based correct version.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one Thread wrapping a settlement sweep, and the same sweep logic submitted three times to a pool.

Step 1: The Thread is constructed and reports its state as NEW, meaning it has been created but not scheduled.

Step 2: The first start is called. This is legal because the thread is in NEW, so it transitions to RUNNABLE, the JVM creates the native thread, and the sweep runs and logs its progress.

Step 3: The main thread joins, waiting for the sweep to finish. When run completes, the thread moves to TERMINATED, which the demo confirms by printing the state.

Step 4: A second start is attempted on the same Thread. Because the thread is now TERMINATED, not NEW, the start method's lifecycle check fails and throws IllegalThreadStateException, which the demo catches and logs with the stack trace.

Step 5: The correct pattern begins. The sweep logic, held as a Runnable, is submitted three times to a fixed thread pool of two worker threads. The pool runs each submission on a reusable worker, so the same logic executes three times with no lifecycle error.

Step 6: The pool is shut down and awaited, and the demo logs that all pooled sweeps completed, demonstrating that reuse belongs at the executor level while each raw Thread is started only once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Calling start a second time on the same Thread object throws IllegalThreadStateException, and the reason is that a Thread is a one-shot object with a strictly one-directional lifecycle. A newly constructed Thread is in the NEW state. The first start transitions it to RUNNABLE, creates the underlying native thread, and runs its run method, and when run finishes the thread moves to TERMINATED. There is no path back to NEW from any later state. The start method is defined to be legal only from the NEW state, so it checks the thread's state and throws IllegalThreadStateException, an unchecked exception, whenever the thread is no longer NEW. That happens both if you call start again while the thread is still running and if you call it again after the thread has terminated, so the failure is deterministic and about the lifecycle precondition, not about timing.

A key clarification I always make is the difference between calling start twice and calling run twice. The run method is just an ordinary method with no lifecycle check, so you can call it any number of times, but calling run directly does not start a new thread at all, it executes the body synchronously on the calling thread. The lifecycle protection lives entirely in start, which is why calling run when you meant start is a classic concurrency bug.

The design is one-shot because a Thread is bound to a native operating-system thread and a specific execution context, and reusing one Thread object for multiple independent runs would badly complicate state, thread-local storage, naming, and interruption. So Java separates the work from the worker: you express the work as a Runnable or Callable and submit it to an ExecutorService, which keeps a pool of reusable worker threads. The pool runs your task and returns the worker for the next task, so reuse happens at the pool level while each individual Thread is still started only once internally. That is why in production I almost never create and start raw Thread objects.

In a project at National Bank of India an early nightly settlement sweep created a single Thread and, for a retry, called start on that same Thread again, which threw IllegalThreadStateException and aborted the retry. The fix was to move the sweep logic into a Runnable and submit it to an executor, using a scheduled executor for the recurring nightly runs and the same pool for retries, so the sweep could run as many times as needed on reusable workers with no lifecycle error. The principle I state is that a Thread can be started exactly once, you never try to restart it, and whenever you need to run the same logic repeatedly you keep it as a task and hand it to an executor, which also bounds resource usage, rather than keeping and restarting a raw Thread.

---

keyPoints: A Thread can only be started ONCE — it cannot return to NEW state
After termination, the Thread object exists but cannot be restarted
To run again: create a new Thread object with the same Runnable
